title: Consistency Models
summary: The menu of promises replicated systems make about reads, from linearizable to causal to eventual, and how quorum math R + W > N tunes them.

questions.prompt: A user updates their profile photo, refreshes, and sees the old photo; refreshing again shows the new one. What's happening, and which consistency guarantees are being violated?
questions.hint: Think about which replica each read lands on.
keyPoints: Writes go to one replica (leader) and replicate asynchronously; reads hit different replicas with different lag
Read-your-writes is violated: the user doesn't see their own write
Monotonic reads is violated if they see new then old again
The system is likely only eventually consistent
questions.answer:
The database uses **leader-based replication with asynchronous followers**. The photo update was written to the leader, but followers apply it a little later (**replication lag**). The first refresh's read was routed to a follower that hadn't caught up yet, so it returned the old photo; the second refresh hit a follower (or the leader) that had.

Guarantees violated:

- **Read-your-writes**: a user should always see their own updates after making them. Here they didn't.
- **Monotonic reads**: once you've seen a newer value, you should never see an older one again. If the user saw the **new** photo and then the **old** one on a later refresh (bouncing between a fresh and a lagging replica), that's a monotonic-reads violation too.

The system as a whole is only **eventually consistent**: replicas converge if writes stop, but nothing is promised about reads in between. Fixes: read a user's own data from the leader for a short window after writing, and pin each user to one replica.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between linearizability, causal consistency and eventual consistency, with one real feature that needs each.
questions.hint: Single copy and real time; cause before effect; converges eventually.
keyPoints: Linearizable: behaves like one copy; once a write completes every later read sees it (real-time order). Example: unique username, lock, last seat
Causal: causally related operations seen in the same order by everyone; concurrent ones may differ. Example: replies never shown before the post/comment they answer
Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop, no promise on interim reads. Example: like counts, view counters, DNS
Stronger models cost latency/availability; causal is the strongest that can stay available during partitions
questions.answer:
**Linearizability** (strong consistency): the system behaves as if there's **one copy** of the data. Once a write completes, **every** later read, by anyone, sees it, in real-time order.
*Needs it*: **unique usernames**, a distributed **lock**, selling the **last seat**. Two people must never both "win".

**Causal consistency**: operations that are **causally related** (one could have influenced the other, like a reply to a post) are seen **in the same order by everyone**. **Concurrent** (unrelated) operations may appear in different orders on different replicas.
*Needs it*: **comments and replies**. A reply must never be shown before the comment it answers.

**Eventual consistency**: if writes stop, replicas **eventually converge** to the same value. Meanwhile, reads may return stale or out-of-order values.
*Fine for*: **like counts**, view counters, DNS. Showing 1,203 likes instead of 1,205 harms no one.

Trade-off: stronger models need more coordination between replicas, which costs **latency** and **availability**. Linearizability can't stay available during a partition (CAP), while **causal consistency is the strongest model that can stay available** during a partition.

questions.prompt: A leaderless store has N = 5 replicas per key. (a) Pick R and W so every read overlaps every write and both reads and writes survive 2 failed nodes. (b) If instead you set W = 5, R = 1, how many failures can reads and writes each survive? (c) Is W = 2, R = 3 a valid overlapping quorum?
questions.hint: Overlap needs R + W > N. Writes survive N − W failures; reads survive N − R.
keyPoints: (a) Need W ≤ 3 and R ≤ 3 for 2 failures, and R + W ≥ 6, so W = 3, R = 3
(b) Writes tolerate 5 − 5 = 0 failures; reads tolerate 5 − 1 = 4
(c) 2 + 3 = 5, which is not > 5, so no: a read can miss every replica that has the latest write
Overlap means at least one replica in any read set has the latest successful write
questions.answer:
(a) `W = 3, R = 3`: `3 + 3 = 6 > 5`, and each tolerates `5 − 3 = 2` failures.

(b) Writes: `5 − 5 = 0` failures tolerated (any node down blocks writes). Reads: `5 − 1 = 4`.

(c) `2 + 3 = 5`, not `> 5`. The write could land on replicas {1,2} and the read hit {3,4,5}: no overlap, stale read possible.

questions.prompt: In your forum app, users sometimes see a reply ("Totally agree!") appear before the post it replies to. Name the anomaly and the consistency model that prevents it, and suggest a way to implement it.
questions.hint: The reply was written after reading the post. What relationship is that?
keyPoints: Violation of causal consistency (also called consistent prefix / causality anomaly)
The reply causally depends on the post, so everyone must see the post first
Implement by tracking dependencies: attach the parent's id/version (or vector clock) to the reply and don't show it until the dependency is visible
Alternatives: route the thread to the same partition/replica so it's applied in order
questions.answer:
This is a **causality violation**: a **causal consistency** anomaly (also described as a **consistent prefix** violation, where you see a later part of history without the earlier part it depends on). The reply "Totally agree!" **causally depends** on the post: its author read the post first. So every reader must see the post **before** the reply.

It happens when the post and reply are written to (or replicated through) different replicas/partitions with different lag, and the reader's replica got the reply first.

**Preventing it (causal consistency):**

- **Track dependencies**: store the parent's id and version (or a **vector clock**) with each reply, e.g. `{ replyId: 77, parentId: 12, parentVersion: 3 }`. A replica **doesn't show the reply** until the post it depends on is visible there (buffer it, or hide it until the parent arrives).
- **Alternative**: route the entire thread to the **same partition / replica** (shard by `threadId`). Writes to one partition are applied in a single order, so the post always lands before its replies.

questions.prompt: You read from R replicas, each returning `{ version, value }`. Write a JavaScript function `resolveRead(responses, replicas)` that returns the newest value and also performs **read repair**: any replica that returned an older version gets updated. Assume `responses[i]` came from `replicas[i]`, and each replica has a `write(version, value)` method.
questions.hint: Find the max version first, then loop again.
keyPoints: Pick the response with the highest version as the result
Compare each response's version to the newest
Call write(newest.version, newest.value) on replicas that returned an older version
Return the newest value to the caller
Read repair helps stale replicas converge without waiting for background anti-entropy

questions.prompt: You're designing a social network's storage. For each feature, choose the weakest consistency model that still gives a good user experience, and say how you'd implement it: (a) signing up with a unique username, (b) a user's own new post showing in their profile, (c) comments on a post, (d) the like counter.
questions.hint: Weaker is cheaper and more available; go stronger only where users would notice or data would be wrong.
keyPoints: (a) Linearizable: single leader / consensus-backed unique constraint, or a conditional write
(b) Read-your-writes: read from the leader for a short window after writing, or client sends last-write version so the replica waits/redirects until caught up
(c) Causal: replies carry dependency info so they aren't shown before their parent; per-thread ordering
(d) Eventual: async counters (sharded or batched), approximate values acceptable
Justifies each choice by the cost of anomalies vs latency/availability
questions.answer:
The guiding idea: stronger consistency costs **latency and availability**, so use the **weakest model whose anomalies users wouldn't tolerate**.

**(a) Unique username: Linearizable.** Two people must never both get `@kim`, and an anomaly here is permanent. Implement with a **single leader / consensus-backed** store and a **unique constraint**, or a **conditional write** ("insert if not exists"). Signup is rare, so the extra few ms is fine.

**(b) Own new post on own profile: Read-your-writes.** Only the **author** must see it immediately (a missing post looks like a bug and they'd repost); followers can see it a few seconds later. Implement by reading from the **leader for a short window** (e.g. 10 s) after the user writes, or have the client send its **last-write version** so a replica waits or redirects until it has caught up.

**(c) Comments: Causal.** Replies must never appear before what they reply to, but unrelated comments can arrive in any order. Implement by attaching **dependency info** (parent id/version) to each reply and not showing it until the parent is visible, plus **per-thread ordering** (shard by post id).

**(d) Like counter: Eventual.** "1,203" vs "1,205" for a few seconds hurts no one, and likes are high-volume. Implement with **async counters**: sharded counters summed periodically, or batched increments via a queue; approximate values are acceptable.

Each step down (a → d) trades away guarantees exactly where the anomaly is cheap, which keeps the system fast and available where it matters.
